headline: Across the full 1,491-industry corpus in 2025-2026, labor scarcity, demographic aging, consumer bifurcation, AI buildout, compliance load, channel migration, and consolidation keep repricing who captures demand, who gets squeezed, and which operators can actually turn growth into durable economics.

trends.name: AI adoption and labor displacement
trends.what_it_is: AI tools are automating routine cognitive and physical work across every sector—from accounting to medical diagnostics to creative services. Winners deploy AI fast and retain workers in higher-value roles; losers face talent exodus and margin collapse.
industries: US Business Analytics & Enterprise Software Publishing

US Data Processing and Hosting Services

US Credit Bureaus & Rating Agencies Industry

US Business Certification & IT Schools Industry
Weight Loss Services in the US
trends.who_wins: Firms that invest in AI for productivity and retrain workers for higher-value work stay profitable; firms that deploy it only to cut headcount face skill collapse.
trends.who_loses: Routine service providers (data entry, junior consulting, basic diagnostics) and firms that can't afford AI tooling lose pricing power and talent.

structural_tensions: The central tension inside Machine Intelligence and Compute Buildout is that AI is not just a software feature cycle. It is simultaneously a workflow-compression story, a compute and power infrastructure story, and a market concentration story around who can afford the stack, but the route to capturing that demand runs through the practical frictions surfaced by The Data-Center Land Rush Creates New Scarcity.
A second tension sits between household or institutional demand and the operating constraints surfaced by Workflow Compression Rewrites Knowledge Work.

The central tension inside Work Without the Old Firm is that the traditional firm is thinning. Expertise is rented more often, junior pathways are weaker, benefits are externalized, and automation is increasingly used to defend margins against labor scarcity, but the route to capturing that demand runs through the practical frictions surfaced by The Fractional Executive Layer Expands.
signals_to_watch: Automation budgets, inference demand, and power-ready site competition keep rising.
Advisory retainers, project staffing, and portable admin layers gain relevance.
Automation, scheduling discipline, retention tactics, and selective simplification accelerate.
second_order_effects: In Colocation Facilities, this tends to show up as a second-order consequence where AI infrastructure demand has turned the colocation industry from a physical space problem into a power-grid problem, making electricity access and regulatory tariffs the new competitive moats.

In Business Analytics & Enterprise Software Publishing in the US, this tends to show up as a second-order consequence where AI agents are destroying the software industry's traditional value propositions while forcing massive consolidation and pricing model shifts, making 2026 a year of existential reckoning for mid-market vendors.

In Internet Hosting Services, this tends to show up as a second-order consequence where AI automation, cloud encroachment, and consolidation are reshaping a slowing market where traditional hosting providers fight margin pressure while adapting to enterprise demands for security, privacy, and sustainability.

trends.name: Tariff-driven cost shock and supply chain upheaval
trends.what_it_is: Tariffs (25-54% on China imports, USMCA reciprocal duties) are raising input costs across manufacturing, retail, and trade. Companies are scrambling to nearshore to Mexico, Vietnam, or India while trying to pass costs through to consumers. Margins are getting squeezed.

trends.who_wins: Nearshore-reliant manufacturers (Mexico-based assembly) and value brands that lock in tariff-resistant price elasticity; companies with hedged supply chains survive.
trends.who_loses: Importers with thin margins (retail, food, components), companies unable to pass through costs, and small suppliers lacking negotiating power.

In Colocation Facilities, this tends to show up as a second-order consequence where AI infrastructure demand has turned the colocation industry from a physical space problem into a power-grid problem, making electricity access and regulatory tariffs the new competitive moats.

trends.name: Reimbursement pressure and pricing power collapse
trends.what_it_is: Across healthcare, Medicare cuts are eroding margins; insurance companies and hospital systems are squeezing suppliers and service providers. Wage inflation outpaces reimbursement growth, forcing closures and consolidation.

trends.who_loses: Solo practitioners, small medical practices, and independent clinics; specialists without volume; any provider reliant on a single payer.

A second tension sits between household or institutional demand and the operating constraints surfaced by Senior Housing Demand Meets Staffing and Capacity Friction.

The central tension inside Regulated Software and the Admin State is that a larger share of economic value now comes from managing mandatory complexity: compliance, identity, reimbursement, audit trails, fraud control, privacy, testing, and other workflows customers cannot simply skip, but the route to capturing that demand runs through the practical frictions surfaced by Compliance Itself Becomes a Demand Engine.
signals_to_watch: Demand tilts toward chronic care, assistance, protection, and age-adapted convenience.
Margin performance diverges more from volume growth in payer-shaped sectors.

In Residential Senior Care Franchises, this tends to show up as a second-order consequence where residential senior care franchises operate small assisted-living homes, memory-care homes and continuing-care settings that generate revenue from private-pay resident fees, entrance fees and limited Medicare or Medicaid reimbursements.

trends.who_loses: Legacy office landlords and tenants; retail real estate; suburban office parks; small commercial landlords.

trends.name: Gig economy and fractional work blurring permanent employment
trends.what_it_is: Contractors, fractional roles, and gig platforms are normalizing across consulting, executive search, and creative services. Permanent employment is declining; benefits and stability are eroding. Workers are diversifying income sources.
trends.who_wins: Platforms connecting gig workers and fractional roles; consulting firms pivoting to advisory and interim placements; niche specialists.
trends.who_loses: Permanent corporate staffing models; job security in traditional roles; benefits-dependent workers.
subthemes: The Fractional Executive Layer Expands
Skills and Credentials Replace Slow Career Ladders
The Junior Rung Gets Compressed
structural_tensions: The central tension inside Work Without the Old Firm is that the traditional firm is thinning. Expertise is rented more often, junior pathways are weaker, benefits are externalized, and automation is increasingly used to defend margins against labor scarcity, but the route to capturing that demand runs through the practical frictions surfaced by The Fractional Executive Layer Expands.
A second tension sits between household or institutional demand and the operating constraints surfaced by Skills and Credentials Replace Slow Career Ladders.
signals_to_watch: Advisory retainers, project staffing, and portable admin layers gain relevance.
Automation, scheduling discipline, retention tactics, and selective simplification accelerate.
second_order_effects: In Business Coaching in the US, this tends to show up as a second-order consequence where business coaching in 2025-2026 is shifting from a discretionary C-suite perk to a scaled, AI-augmented professional development tool for mid-market and small-business leaders, underpinned by measured ROI claims and driven by a fragmented but rapidly professionalizing workforce of 165,000+ coaches.

In Business Certification & IT Schools in the US, this tends to show up as a second-order consequence where the US business certification and IT schools industry is bifurcating: high-margin enterprise and compliance-linked credentials (cloud, cybersecurity) are growing at 12-16% annually, while commodity bootcamps and general IT courses face bankruptcies and commoditization as AI and free learning platforms make basic skills training structurally uncompetitive.

In Accounting Services in the US, this tends to show up as a second-order consequence where the US accounting services market is in structural transition, with AI automation and labor scarcity fragmenting the middle market and accelerating consolidation by private equity, while the Big Four use technology and service expansion to hold and grow their dominant position.

trends.name: Alternative ownership: PE, REIT, and institutional capital reshaping industries
trends.what_it_is: Private equity is rolling up fragmented service industries (dental, health, fitness, restaurants). REITs are consolidating real estate. Sovereign wealth and institutional investors are buying real assets (catalogs, infrastructure, land). This favors scale and operational discipline but squeezes margins and cuts independent ownership.

structural_tensions: The central tension inside Scale, Financialization, and the Owned Economy is that more of the economy is being shaped by scale owners, roll-up logic, institutional asset holders, and platform economics that centralize purchasing power, compliance, and capital access, but the route to capturing that demand runs through the practical frictions surfaced by Roll-Ups Colonize Essential Services.
A second tension sits between household or institutional demand and the operating constraints surfaced by Asset Owners Keep Gaining Relative Power.

The central tension inside Space, Housing, and Local Friction is that where Americans live, commute, and locate activity is being reorganized by housing lock-in, office impairment, land scarcity near infrastructure, and the uneven value of local place, but the route to capturing that demand runs through the practical frictions surfaced by Office Obsolescence Is a Structural Shift.
signals_to_watch: Platform control, roll-ups, and centralized purchasing keep widening the gap.
Verification, underwriting precision, and workflow adjacency become stronger moats.
Adaptive reuse, housing lock-in, and power-adjacent land become recurring decision points.
second_order_effects: In Dentists in the US, this tends to show up as a second-order consequence where the US dental market, worth $196 billion in 2026, is consolidating rapidly as reimbursement stagnation and workforce shortages push independent practitioners into DSO networks while technology and aging populations provide modest growth.

In Land Leasing in the US, this tends to show up as a second-order consequence where a steady, consolidating landlord business serving price-constrained renters, now accelerating because housing is unaffordable and supply is stuck.

In Commercial Banking in the US, this tends to show up as a second-order consequence where commercial Banking in the US consists of FDIC-insured and federally supervised banks that gather deposits, extend consumer and business credit, hold securities, process payments and earn revenue from net interest income plus service, trading, wealth, card and advisory fees.
